articles.title: Oasis, auteurs and seven hours of Bertolucci: 12 unmissable movies from Venice film festival
articles.summary: A backstage peek at the reunion tour and a new film from Burning director Lee Chang-dong are among this year’s most anticipated – plus offerings from Danny Boyle, Luca Guadagnino, Martin McDonagh and more.
body: Danny Boyle’s movie, adapted by James Graham from his own play, is a primal scene of modern Britain and its agonies over class, culture and empire. Rupert Murdoch buys the Sun newspaper in 1969 and turns it into a raucous circulation powerhouse of sexist smut and Tory politics, while gloating over the timid British establishment who winced at the colonial Australian press baron. Guy Pearce plays Murdoch and Jack O’Connell plays editor Larry Lamb.

Here is the latest episode – drawn from hundreds of hours of experimental immersive improv footage filmed in Ukraine 15 years ago – in a colossal and controversial multimedia movie project so epic and bizarre that it’s still hard to believe it actually exists. Russian director Ilya Khrzhanovsky has created a new filmic part of his massive portrait of the Soviet scientist Lev Landau (or “Dau”) and his 60s experimental psychology unit, in which he experiences sexual angst and ponders the possibility of love within a totalitarian society.

articles.title: Ukrainian film-maker criticises EU after it cuts Venice Biennale funding over Russia controversy
articles.summary: Sergei Loznitsa likens removal of €2m grant to ‘a punishment in kindergarten’ on eve of Venice film festival. One of Ukraine’s most acclaimed film-makers has criticised the European Commission’s decision to cut off funds to the Venice Biennale over the opening of Russia’s pavilion, likening it to…
body: The Biennale drew heavy criticism this spring when it allowed Russia to use its pavilion for the first time since 2022, despite the ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Speaking on the eve of the Biennale’s cinematic branch, the Venice film festival, the director Sergei Loznitsa said that while he would “never ever” personally visit the Russian pavilion, the row was a distraction from the EU’s own failure to enforce more effective economic sanctions against Moscow.

“The question I ask myself is this: can the existence of this Russian pavilion stop this war or not?” said Loznitsa, who won wide acclaim for his 2014 documentary Maidan and last year’s Soviet-set drama Two Prosecutors, and is showing his new film Imperium out of competition on the Lido this year.

He added: “What I do know is that in the second quarter of this year, European companies imported gas from Russia at unprecedented levels, and all that money goes straight into bombs that fall on Ukraine.”

articles.title: Hungry review – hippo horror sees multi-ton mammal run amok among bayou boat-trippers
articles.summary: A group of thinly drawn characters on a Louisiana tour fight for survival against a rampaging vegetarian. This animal-attack horror plugs a gap with beasties – hippopotamuses – that may be deadly in real life but are hard to take seriously as a threat on screen.
body: The film naturally spends less time worrying about the hippos’ motives and dwells more on the victims, who look pretty doomed given their thin characterisations. This lot certainly weren’t expecting to be attacked by a hippo when they woke up because they are on a bayou tour in Louisiana, where the biggest threats are normally alligators.

Easily winning girl-least-likely-to-get-hippotomised because she’s nice is Sistine (Madison Davenport) – an all-American cute ingenue who has come along with her sassy best friend Hannah (Olivia Bernstone), who is mainly focused on hunky tour guide Rodrigo (Michel Curiel). Also on board the boat are an assortment of folk with varying degrees of likability, including a retired fireman (Jim Meskimen), his middle-aged daughter (Samantha Coughlan), her teenage son (River Codack), and finally a career lady (Tracey Bonner) clad in very bayou-unfriendly suit and stilettos.

articles.title: The year of Domhnall Gleeson: ‘No one talks about actors’ dedication. But I had a perm for five months!’
articles.summary: He started in the Harry Potter films and has since become ubiquitous, playing every type of character: romcom leads, evil villains, comical idiots. He even starred in a Taylor Swift video. So how does he stay so under the radar?
body: Domhnall Gleeson has got so much new stuff coming up, someone recently joked that this was the “summer of Domhnall”. Now the phrase is all over the internet, and Gleeson is mortified: “The worry is that somebody will say this to me now thinking that I believe it.” He doesn’t know where it came from – possibly his co-star Gayle Rankin on his new movie The Incomer. “It’s certainly not something I’m trying to push … but it would be great if it could be the headline.”

He’s in a good mood when we meet at a London hotel on a hot afternoon. You could say he’s good at interviews – charming, funny, garrulous, the perfect chatshow guest. He could just be acting, admittedly, but he seems to be a genuinely good-natured, grounded sort of guy.

The Incomer, an eccentric Scottish comedy, is one of three new projects Gleeson has coming out in a matter of weeks. The others are the second season of the US Office spin-off The Paper and Werner Herzog’s new film, Bucking Fastard, which is about to play at the Venice film festival. More of all this later, but first we must address Gleeson’s most prominent, and least probable, recent role: as the star of a Taylor Swift music video.

articles.title: Martin Scorsese Mentee Celina Murga Preps Next Pic, ‘The Rehearsals’
articles.summary: Among the 15 projects participating in the upcoming San Sebastián Europe-Latin America Co-Production Forum is “The Rehearsals” (“Los Ensayos”) by Argentina’s Celina Murga, best known for her Martin Scorsese-executive produced dramas ‘The Freshly Cut Grass’ and ‘The Third Side of the River’ and of…
body: “The film reflects on the way our society looks at aging, deterioration and death. We live in a culture that rewards youth and productivity, making aging bodies and slowing time increasingly invisible. Yet confronting mortality can also open new forms of intimacy and a renewed perception of vitality. ‘The Rehearsals’ was born from the desire to make these experiences visible and to ask what we lose when we deny our finite condition,” Murga told Variety.
She plans to shoot the film in Uruguay by 2028 and will make use of its newly introduced audiovisual tax credit on up to 30% of eligible expenditures in the country.

Currently consolidating its international co-production and financing structure, the project counts on Uruguay-based Alterna Media, which will lead the local production. Alterna Media’s Maria Laura Berch, Joaquin Romero Vercellino and Lucia Vela serve as executive producers.

articles.title: ‘The Runner’ Review: Gal Gadot Is a Mother on a Rescue Mission in an Energetic but Uninspired Amazon Thriller
articles.summary: A frantic journey across London on foot provides a lot of exercise for Gal Gadot, but not much reward for viewers, in “The Runner.” Hardly the first thriller centering on an exceptionally action-ready parent surmounting various obstacles to rescue an imperiled child from some diabolical abductor…
body: In director Kevin Macdonald’s flashy if over-familiar Prime Original, Gadot tours London at an athletic pace, in pursuit of her imperiled child.

Maia Marten (Gadot) is an emigre single mother packing her approximately eight-year-old son Noah (Rory Wilmot, also in the forthcoming “Harry Potter” HBO series) off to school before her own big day. A lawyer with a top firm, she’s on the team prosecuting a notorious crime boss for the murder of two women, and today is the day their heavily guarded star witness (Phoenix Di Sebastiani) will testify.

We have already noticed, though Maia has not, that her phone has been hacked by some outside player. She figures that out soon enough, however, when she’s just commenced her pre-work morning run —receiving a call from her son’s phone, only it’s not Noah on the line. Instead, it’s a sneeringly in-control adult male voice ( Damian Lewis ), who’s apparently been spying on the small family for a while. Not only does he know all about them and their daily habits, he’s already whisked the too-trusting boy from school grounds.

articles.title: Semi-pro football club 'in shock' after shirt worn by Reading Festival headliners
articles.summary: The club says sales of the shirt almost doubled after it was worn by Fontaines D.C frontman Grian Chatten.
body: A semi-professional Welsh football club say they were "in shock" after their shirt was worn during a Reading Festival headline set.

Grian Chatten, frontman of the Irish five-piece band Fontaines D.C., was seen sporting a green and white-striped Cwmbran Celtic away shirt during the performance on Friday, leading to pre-sales of the shirt to "almost double".
In a post shared on social media, the club said "we're still in shock and can't thank Grian enough for the support".
Sales of the shirt go both towards supporting the club as well as to grassroots music venues, with the club having partnered with four famous bands for their 2026/27 season team kits.

articles.title: Hyun Bin and Woo Do-hwan Turn Against Each Other in Hulu and Disney+’s ‘Made in Korea’ Season 2
articles.summary: At a some KRW70 billion ($51 million) across two seasons, “Made in Korea” ranks among the most expensive K-dramas ever made. Season 2 premieres six episodes on Hulu and Disney+ Sept. 9, closing the story in 1979, the year Korean politics came apart in 10 weeks.
body: The gap was a deliberate choice. “Nine years seemed like an appropriate number of years, and it’s a long period of time that can change people significantly,” says Woo. Besides history, the main draw of the season is how changed all the characters are. Ki-tae is now second-in-command at the KCIA, closer than he has ever been to the top job. “While rising through the ranks, he has met and dealt with many people and his methods have changed,” says Hyun Bin (“Crash Landing on You,” “Harbin”), who plays Baek Ki-tae. The character’s wealth and status have reshaped his relationships and the way he treats the people around him.

That drift is what drives the season’s central conflict: the widening gap between Ki-tae and his younger brother, Baek Ki-hyun, the once-timid recruit now risen through military ranks. Woo Do-hwan (“Bloodhounds,” “Mr. Plankton”), who plays Baek Ki-hyun, says his character’s social position has changed and he has gained some power of his own, allowing him to talk back to his brother more, adding, “His beliefs have become stronger.”

articles.title: ‘The Indies’ Goes on a Journey With 3 Men Taking a Painting Across a Europe Ravaged by Conflicts (Exclusive Venice Trailer)
articles.summary: The period road movie, the debut fiction feature from Pauline Julier and Nicolas Chapoulier, premieres in the Venice Days program, using a historical lens to examine the origins of the world we inhabit today.
body: In 1652, Spanish artist Diego Velázquez painted the portrait of Maria Theresa of Austria, Infanta of Spain. “Infanta” was a royal title given to the daughters of a monarch who were not the direct heir to the throne. A few weeks later, the painting reached the court of Louis XIV, who was still a child, sealing the union of the French and Spanish monarchies, as well as peace after the Thirty Years’ War.

“In our own time, when images circulate instantaneously, imagining the creation and transport of this painting, and its political significance, struck us as a powerful dramatic engine,” the co-directors share in a directors’ note. “It is the 17th century: the medieval era is fading in the face of the rise of science, rationalism, and commerce. The world is no longer merely to be explored – it is to be conquered.”

articles.title: Venice First Look: Toni Servillo Meets His Match in Mario Martone’s ‘Scherzetto’
articles.summary: The Italian screen legend plays a solitary illustrator thrown into battle with his unruly five-year-old grandson in the feature adaptation of Domenico Starnone’s novel.
body: A mordant Toni Servillo may have met his match in this exclusive early image from Scherzetto, director Mario Martone’s feature adaptation of an Italian novel of the same name by author Domenico Starnone.

Scherzetto will premiere out of competition at the Venice Film Festival on Sept 10. The project’s sales agent, Rai Cinema, shared a first-look still (above) with The Hollywood Reporter shortly before the festival’s opening.

A Lido regular and pillar of contemporary Italian cinema and theater generally, Martone made his feature debut with Death of a Neapolitan Mathematician, which won Venice’s grand jury prize in 1992. His last feature at the festival was the 2021 competition entry Qui rido io, another collaboration with Servillo. For his part, Servillo, a lion of the Italian stage and screen, arrives back in Venice just one year after winning the festival’s Volpi Cup for best actor for his performance in Paolo Sorrentino’s La Grazia.
